title: How to apply for UGC jobs as a beginner
description: Build a focused UGC application with relevant samples, a reusable profile, and questions that clarify the brief before you agree to the work.
content:
## What belongs in a UGC job application?

A useful UGC application contains relevant work samples, a short explanation of how you fit the brief, your availability, and any requested eligibility details. Follow the listing's instructions. If payment, deliverables, or usage are unclear, ask for those terms before agreeing to the project.

On [ugc.community](/jobs), creators can browse reviewed opportunities without signing in. An account lets you save a [reusable application profile](/apply-profile) and work links for jobs that accept email applications through the site. Other listings use the original application destination.

## Step 1: Choose a brief you can fulfill

Read the requirements before preparing a pitch. Check the product category, filming location, language, deadlines, deliverables, and any audience or posting requirements. A remote role can still have country restrictions for product shipping or campaign eligibility.

If you need fixed payment, start with [guaranteed cash opportunities](/jobs?pay=cash). Do not treat affiliate commissions, performance bonuses, or gifted products as a substitute for a stated cash fee. A listing with unspecified compensation needs clarification.

Use the [job discovery guide](/tutorials/find-paid-ugc-jobs) to compare opportunities across boards, brand pages, casting calls, and outreach.

## Step 2: Select samples that answer the brief

Choose a small set of relevant samples rather than sending every video you have made. A skincare demonstration, an app walkthrough, and a food preparation video show different skills. Match your examples to the requested format and explain your role in making them.

If you have no client work, you can create a practice sample using a product you already own. Label it as a practice or independently produced sample so the brand can distinguish it from commissioned work. Do not imply a past brand relationship or invent performance results.

For each sample, make it easy to see:

- The finished video through a working, viewable link.
- What you handled, such as scripting, filming, voiceover, or editing.
- Why it relates to the brief.
- Any results you can substantiate, if results are relevant and you have permission to share them.

Open your links in a signed out browser before submitting. A private file or expired sharing link prevents the hiring team from evaluating the work.

## Step 3: Write a short, specific application

Use this template as a starting point and replace the bracketed details:

> Hello [hiring contact], I am applying for [role or campaign]. I create [relevant format or subject], and these samples show [specific skill the brief requests]: [sample links]. I can deliver [requested scope] within [your actual availability]. I meet [relevant eligibility requirements]. Could you confirm [missing term]? Thank you, [name and preferred contact].

Keep claims factual. If the listing requests a rate, quote the scope your rate covers and identify anything that needs a separate agreement. If it requests a particular subject line or form, use it.

## Step 4: Use the correct application route

| Listing route | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Email application through ugc.community | Sign in, complete your reusable profile, and review the application before submitting |
| External form or website | Follow the original destination and its instructions |
| Terms or destination are unclear | Contact the hiring party through a verified channel or report the listing for review |

The public jobs API and MCP tools are for reading listings. They do not submit applications. Hiring teams control their own decisions and response times; applying through the site does not guarantee a reply.

## Step 5: Clarify the agreement before production

Ask for the final deliverables, revision scope, payment schedule, usage duration, and any exclusivity or posting requirements in writing. If the brand requests an unpaid custom sample, clarify what it can use and decide whether the work is appropriate for you before making it.

Use the [compensation checklist](/tutorials/compare-ugc-compensation) to compare the offer with the workload. Keep a record of the agreed scope and the application destination so you can follow up in context.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I apply without previous brand clients?

You can apply to briefs whose requirements you meet. Clearly labeled practice samples can demonstrate your skills, but the hiring party decides whether your experience fits. There is no guaranteed path from a first application to a paid project.

### Should I send the same application to every brand?

Reuse your accurate profile details and work links, then tailor the samples and explanation to each brief. An application for an app tutorial should explain relevant screen recording or demonstration skills rather than an unrelated product niche.

### Do I need to buy a course or equipment before applying?

ugc.community does not require a course purchase to browse jobs. Check each brief's production requirements and assess whether your current setup can meet them. Avoid buying equipment solely on the assumption that an application will be accepted.

### Where do I begin?

[Browse current opportunities](/jobs), pick a brief you can fulfill, and prepare the samples it asks for. Save your [application profile](/apply-profile) if you want to use email applications on supported listings.

title: Community Management & Engagement
description: How to respond to comments, build genuine engagement, and manage your community — the skills that turn viewers into loyal followers and impress brands.
content:
Creating content is only half the job. What happens *after* you post — how you engage with comments, build community, and manage your audience — is what separates good creators from great ones. It's also what brands look for when deciding who to work with.

## Why Engagement Matters

Engagement isn't just a vanity metric. It has real, tangible effects on your success:

### Algorithm impact

Every comment, reply, and interaction on your content signals to the algorithm that people care about your post. The more engagement your video gets in the first 30–60 minutes, the more the platform pushes it to new viewers.

When you reply to comments, you're essentially giving the algorithm *two* engagement signals: the original comment + your response. This creates a loop that drives more visibility.

### Brand relationships

Brands don't just look at your content quality — they look at your engagement rate and *how* you interact with your audience. A creator who responds thoughtfully to comments demonstrates that they:

- Take their work seriously
- Can represent a brand professionally
- Build authentic relationships with their audience
- Drive conversations, not just views

<Highlight emoji="📊" title="Engagement rate matters">
Brands often prefer creators with smaller followings but higher engagement rates (3–6%+) over large accounts with low engagement (under 1%). An engaged audience of 5,000 can be more valuable than a passive audience of 50,000.
</Highlight>

## Comment Response Strategies

Not all comments are created equal. Here's how to handle the most common types you'll encounter — especially when creating UGC for a brand or product.

### Curiosity comments

**What they look like:** "What is that?" / "What app is this?" / "Where can I get that?" / "Link?"

**How to respond:** This is the golden comment. Someone is interested and wants to know more. Respond naturally, like you're telling a friend:

> ✅ *"It's called [product name]! I literally use it every day — it's so good for [specific benefit] 💖"*

> ✅ *"OMG yes! It's [product name]. Honestly it's been a game changer for my [routine/workflow]"*

<Callout variant="tip">
Don't just name the product — add a personal detail about why you love it. This feels natural and reinforces the recommendation. A comment that says "It's ProductX" is far less effective than "It's ProductX! The [specific feature] is what sold me."
</Callout>

### Personal experience shares

**What they look like:** "I've been struggling with [problem] too" / "Same thing happened to me!" / "I've been looking for something like this"

**How to respond:** Connect with them emotionally, then recommend:

> ✅ *"I felt the exact same way! That's honestly what made me try [product] — and it actually helped. You should give it a shot!"*

> ✅ *"Girl, I get it 100%. This is exactly why I started using [product]. Changed everything for me 🙌"*

### Positive comments

**What they look like:** "Just downloaded it!" / "Buying this right now" / "Love this!" / "This looks amazing"

**How to respond:** Celebrate their action and create FOMO for others reading:

> ✅ *"You're going to love it!! Let me know how it goes 🔥"*

> ✅ *"Yesss! Honestly everyone needs [product] in their life. You won't regret it 💕"*

<Callout variant="info">
Every positive reply you write is being read by other viewers scrolling through comments. You're not just responding to one person — you're selling to everyone who reads the thread.
</Callout>

### Questions you can't answer

**What they look like:** "Does this work with [specific condition]?" / "Is this available in [country]?" / "What about [technical question]?"

**How to respond:** Be honest. Don't make things up. If you're working with a brand, check with them first:

> ✅ *"Great question! I'm not 100% sure about that specific thing — let me find out and I'll follow up!"*

> ✅ *"Honestly I haven't tested it for that specific use case, but I'd check their FAQ/website for details 😊"*

### Negative comments

**What they look like:** "This doesn't work" / "Waste of money" / "This is just an ad" / "[rude/trolling comment]"

**How to respond:** This depends on the comment:

- **Constructive criticism:** Address it genuinely. "Sorry it didn't work for you! Everyone's experience is different. For me, [what worked]."
- **Trolling or spam:** Delete it. Don't engage. Your comment section is your space.
- **"It's just an ad" comments:** You can be honest: "I actually use this myself! If I didn't love it, I wouldn't make content about it 🤷‍♀️"

<Callout variant="warning">
Never get into arguments in your comments. It looks unprofessional and brands will notice. If someone is being genuinely rude, delete and move on. If they're raising a fair point, address it gracefully and move on. Your comment section reflects your brand.
</Callout>

### Competitor mentions

**What they look like:** "I prefer [competitor product]" / "[Other product] is better" / "I switched from [competitor] to this"

**How to respond:**

- **If they're positive about a competitor:** Be diplomatic. "I've heard good things about [competitor] too! Personally [product] just worked better for my needs."
- **If they're negative about a competitor:** Don't bash other products. "Glad you found what works for you! For me, [product] has been 💯"
- **If they switched TO your product:** Celebrate it: "Welcome to the club! 🙌 You're going to love the difference."

## The Post-Publish Engagement Ritual

What you do in the 15–30 minutes after posting can make or break a video's performance. Here's the routine:

<Step number={1} title="Post your video">
Upload with captions, hashtags, and sounds ready to go.
</Step>

<Step number={2} title="Engage on your FYP for 5–10 minutes">
Immediately after posting, open your For You Page and interact — like, comment, save videos. This tells the algorithm you're an active, genuine user, not a post-and-ghost bot.
</Step>

<Step number={3} title="Reply to early comments within minutes">
When the first comments come in, reply immediately. Fast replies drive comment threads, which drive engagement, which drives reach.
</Step>

<Step number={4} title="Pin your best comment">
If someone leaves a great comment (funny, positive, asking about the product), pin it. Pinned comments are the first thing new viewers see.
</Step>

<Step number={5} title="Drop a comment yourself">
Leave a comment on your own video with extra info: the product name, a discount code, or a conversation starter. "Has anyone else tried this? What do you think?"
</Step>

<Callout variant="tip">
This 15-minute ritual after every post is non-negotiable if you're serious about growing. It's the difference between a video that gets 500 views and one that gets 50,000.
</Callout>

## Building Genuine Community

There's a difference between "engagement hacking" and building real community. Both matter, but the latter is what creates a sustainable UGC career.

### Be a real person

- Share your genuine opinions, not just what you think brands want to hear
- Admit when something doesn't work for you
- Show your personality — humor, quirks, opinions
- Remember and reference recurring commenters

### Create engagement opportunities

- Ask questions in your captions: "What's your go-to [product type]?"
- Use polls and Q&A stickers in Stories
- Make content directly responding to viewer comments and questions
- Create "part 2" content based on what people ask for

### Support other creators

- Engage with content from creators in your niche
- Leave meaningful comments (not "nice vid 🔥" — actually say something specific)
- Share content from creators you genuinely admire
- Collaborate when opportunities arise

## DM Etiquette

As you grow, you'll get DMs from brands, potential collaborators, and followers. Here's how to handle them:

### Brand DMs

- **Respond within 24 hours.** Brands often reach out to multiple creators simultaneously. The one who responds fastest and most professionally often gets the gig.
- **Be professional but personable.** "Thanks so much for reaching out! I'd love to learn more about what you're looking for. Here's my portfolio: [link]"
- **Ask clarifying questions.** What's the deliverable? Timeline? Compensation? Usage rights?
- **Never accept the first offer without understanding the full scope.** It's okay to ask for details before saying yes.

### Follower DMs

- You don't need to reply to every DM, but respond to genuine questions when you can
- Never share personal information
- If someone is being inappropriate, block and report without hesitation

<Callout variant="info">
Keep your DMs open on all platforms, especially Instagram. Many brand deals start with a DM. If your messages are closed, you're literally turning away money.
</Callout>

## What's Next

Community management is an ongoing practice. Keep refining your approach as your audience grows:

- **[Discoverability](/tutorials/discoverability)** — Get more eyeballs on your content with hashtags and SEO
- **[Hook Library](/tutorials/hook-library)** — Better hooks = more comments = more engagement opportunities
- **[Compensation Guide](/tutorials/compensation-guide)** — When brands reach out, know what you're worth

title: How to compare UGC job pay and deliverables
description: Understand guaranteed cash, variable pay, affiliate commissions, and gifted UGC offers. Compare the full scope using a worked example and questions for brands.
content:
## How do you compare two UGC job offers?

Compare the guaranteed cash amount against the full workload, payment conditions, and requested usage. Keep potential bonuses and commissions separate from fixed payment. The number of videos alone does not capture research, scripting, revisions, travel, raw footage, or posting obligations.

[ugc.community](/jobs) labels compensation so creators can distinguish fixed payment from variable earnings and product exchanges. These labels describe the stated payment structure. They do not establish a market rate, guarantee payment, or tell you whether an offer fits your needs.

## What do the compensation categories mean?

| Board category | How to read it | What to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Guaranteed cash | A stated cash fee for the agreed work | Amount, currency, acceptance criteria, and payment schedule |
| Base plus variable | A fixed amount plus potential additional earnings | Which amount is fixed and what triggers the rest |
| Performance only | Payment depends on stated performance conditions | Measurement window, qualifying events, reporting, and payout rules |
| Affiliate | Earnings depend on tracked referrals or sales | Attribution rules, commission basis, deductions, and payment timing |
| Gifted or unpaid | Product compensation or no stated cash payment | What is provided and whether content or posting is expected |
| Unspecified | The source does not state enough payment information | Ask for the payment structure before treating the role as paid |

The label “guaranteed cash” describes an agreed fee rather than earnings dependent on views or sales. It does not mean ugc.community guarantees the employer will pay. Review the original terms and who is responsible for payment.

## A worked comparison of two hypothetical offers

The following numbers are illustrative arithmetic, not observed creator earnings, recommended rates, or live jobs.

| Term | Offer A | Offer B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed cash | $240 | $360 |
| Finished videos | 2 | 4 |
| Included revisions | One round per video | Two rounds per video |
| Other deliverables | None in this example | Raw footage |
| Potential bonus | None | $120 if stated performance conditions are met |
| Fixed cash per finished video | $120 | $90 |

Offer B has the higher headline fixed payment, but it covers more videos, additional revisions, and raw footage. Its bonus is conditional. Offer A has more fixed cash per finished video in this example, but neither calculation establishes which is better without the usage terms, expected hours, and payment conditions.

To compare your own workload, estimate hours for planning, filming, editing, communication, and revisions. Divide the fixed fee by those estimated hours as a planning aid. Keep expenses and any additional obligations visible rather than treating that calculation as take home earnings.

## Which scope details change the comparison?

Ask the hiring party to specify:

- **Production:** finished video count, duration, formats, hook variations, reshoots, and raw footage.
- **Revisions:** included rounds, what counts as a revision, and what happens when the brief changes.
- **Usage:** organic channels, paid ads, duration, territories, and whether the brand needs advertising permissions through your account.
- **Distribution:** whether you must post to your own channels and keep content live for a set period.
- **Exclusivity:** any limits on working with other brands and how long they last.
- **Payment:** payer, currency, invoicing process, payment trigger, and timing.

These are questions for defining the offer, not assumptions about rights or contract enforceability. If a listing says “not stated,” the board has not supplied a missing term on the employer's behalf.

## How do you filter for the payment structure you want?

Start with [guaranteed cash jobs](/jobs?pay=cash) if you want a stated fixed fee, or [base plus variable jobs](/jobs?pay=mixed) if you are open to bonuses alongside fixed payment. Search results reflect current published listings and may have no matches.

Read the original source before applying. Each ugc.community listing is reviewed before publication, but a review does not verify future earnings or replace your own assessment of the hiring party. See the [job discovery guide](/tutorials/find-paid-ugc-jobs) for source and freshness details.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a good UGC rate?

There is no universal rate established by this guide. Define your production scope, expected hours, expenses, requested usage, and payment conditions before deciding what fee you can accept. A single per video number can hide substantial differences between briefs.

### Is gifted UGC a paid job?

Product compensation is different from a guaranteed cash fee. On ugc.community, gifted or unpaid opportunities have their own category so creators can assess them separately from cash work.

### Does a performance bonus count as guaranteed pay?

No. Count the fixed amount separately and treat a bonus as conditional on the written rules. If there is no fixed amount, do not present possible performance earnings as guaranteed cash.

### What should a brand include in its brief?

State compensation structure, deliverables, eligibility, usage, the application destination, and a closing date. Use the [UGC job brief template](/tutorials/ugc-job-brief-template) to make those terms easier to compare.

## Compare the complete offer

[Browse current UGC jobs](/jobs) and record the fixed fee, workload, and missing terms before applying. Use the [application checklist](/tutorials/apply-for-ugc-jobs) once you find a suitable brief.

title: Understanding UGC Compensation
description: How much UGC creators earn, common payment structures, pricing your work, negotiation tips, and red flags to watch for in brand deals.
content:
Money talk. This is the guide most creators wish they'd had when starting out. Understanding how UGC compensation works — what's fair, what's not, and how to negotiate — is the difference between getting underpaid and building a sustainable creative career.

## The UGC Rate Landscape

UGC rates vary widely depending on experience, niche, deliverables, and usage rights. Here's a realistic overview of what creators earn today.

### Beginner rates (0–6 months experience)

| Deliverable | Typical Range |
|---|---|
| Single short-form video (TikTok/Reels) | $50–$150 |
| Photo set (3–5 images) | $50–$100 |
| Product-only deal (free product for content) | $0 cash (product value varies) |
| Monthly ambassador program | $200–$500/month |

### Intermediate rates (6–18 months, portfolio of proven work)

| Deliverable | Typical Range |
|---|---|
| Single short-form video | $150–$400 |
| Video + usage rights (brand can run as ad) | $250–$600 |
| Photo set (3–5 images) | $100–$250 |
| Monthly retainer (4–8 videos) | $500–$1,500/month |

### Experienced rates (18+ months, viral content track record)

| Deliverable | Typical Range |
|---|---|
| Single short-form video | $400–$1,000+ |
| Video + full usage rights | $600–$2,000+ |
| Photo set | $200–$500 |
| Monthly retainer | $1,500–$5,000+/month |
| Full campaign (multiple deliverables) | $2,000–$10,000+ |

<Callout variant="info">
These ranges are guidelines, not rules. Your rates depend on your niche (finance and tech tend to pay more than lifestyle), your portfolio quality, and your negotiation skills. Don't undervalue your work — but also be realistic about where you are in your journey.
</Callout>

## Common Payment Structures

Understanding the different ways brands pay is crucial for evaluating deals.

### Flat fee per deliverable

The most straightforward model. You agree on a price per video/photo, create the content, and get paid.

**Pros:** Predictable income, clear expectations
**Cons:** No upside if your content goes viral

### Monthly retainer / ambassador programs

A brand pays you a fixed monthly amount for a set number of deliverables. This is the most stable arrangement for creators.

**Typical structure:**
- $400–$2,000+/month
- 4–15 videos per month
- Often includes product shipments
- Usually 3–6 month commitment

**Pros:** Predictable income, deeper brand relationships, less time pitching
**Cons:** Can be demanding, may limit working with competitors

<Highlight emoji="🎯" title="The ambassador sweet spot">
Ambassador/retainer programs are the best deal in UGC. Even at "lower" rates, the consistency and predictability of monthly income often beats higher one-off payments. If a brand offers you a retainer, seriously consider it.
</Highlight>

### Performance bonuses

Some brands offer extra payouts when your content hits view milestones:

- **100K views:** $100–$250 bonus
- **500K views:** $250–$500 bonus
- **1M+ views:** $500–$1,000+ bonus

These are typically *in addition to* your base rate, not instead of it. If a brand offers performance bonuses as the *only* compensation, that's a red flag.

### Affiliate / revenue share

You get a percentage of sales generated through your content, usually tracked via a unique link or discount code.

**Typical rates:** 10–30% commission per sale

**Pros:** Unlimited upside if your content converts well
**Cons:** Income is unpredictable, depends entirely on your content performance

### Product exchange (gifted)

The brand sends you free products in exchange for content. No cash payment.

**When it's worth it:**
- You're brand new and building your portfolio
- The product is something you genuinely want/need (high value)
- The brand has a clear path to a paid relationship later
- You want the content for your own portfolio

**When to say no:**
- You have experience and a solid portfolio
- The product value is low (under $50)
- The brand expects multiple deliverables for a single product
- They're a large, well-funded company that should be paying creators

<Callout variant="warning">
Don't let product exchange become your default. It's fine as a portfolio-building strategy early on, but if you're consistently creating quality content, you should be getting paid. A free $30 product for a video that takes 2 hours to make is not fair compensation.
</Callout>

### Referral bonuses

Many brands pay bonuses for bringing in other creators. Typical range: $50–$200 per referred creator who joins and produces content.

This is easy money — if you know other creators who'd be a good fit, make the introduction. It's a win for everyone.

## Pricing Your Work

Knowing your rates is one thing. Confidently communicating them is another.

### Factors that affect your rate

- **Experience and portfolio quality** — More proven work = higher rates
- **Niche** — Finance, tech, and health tend to pay more than general lifestyle
- **Usage rights** — Will the brand use your content as a paid ad? That costs extra
- **Exclusivity** — Can you work with competitors? Exclusivity = higher rate
- **Deliverable complexity** — A simple product showcase vs. a scripted multi-scene video
- **Timeline** — Rush jobs should cost 25–50% more
- **Number of revisions** — Specify this upfront (1–2 rounds is standard)

### The pricing formula

A simple starting point for per-video pricing:

> **Base rate** (your time + skill) + **Usage rights premium** (if applicable) + **Exclusivity premium** (if applicable) = **Your rate**

**Example for an intermediate creator:**
- Base rate: $200
- Brand wants to run as a paid ad (usage rights): +$150
- Brand wants 30-day competitor exclusivity: +$100
- **Total: $450 per video**

### How to communicate your rates

When a brand asks for your rates, be direct:

> *"Thanks for reaching out! I'd love to work together. For a single short-form video, my rate is $[X]. If you're looking for a package or ongoing partnership, I can offer adjusted pricing. Happy to discuss what works best for both of us!"*

<Callout variant="tip">
Always quote slightly higher than your minimum. If your floor is $200, quote $250–$300. This gives you room to negotiate without going below what you're comfortable with. Most brands expect some negotiation.
</Callout>

## Payment Platforms & Invoicing

Get comfortable with the business side. You're a freelance professional — act like one.

### Common payment methods

- **PayPal** — Most widely used for UGC payments. Easy invoicing.
- **Venmo / Cash App** — Quick and simple for smaller payments.
- **Bank transfer / wire** — More common with larger brands and agencies.
- **Payment platforms** — Some brands use dedicated payment platforms for creator programs.
- **Invoicing tools** — Wave, PayPal Invoicing, or even a simple Google Docs template.

### Invoicing basics

Always send an invoice, even for small payments. It's professional and creates a paper trail. Include:

- Your name and contact info
- The brand/company name
- Description of deliverables
- Agreed-upon rate
- Payment terms (when it's due — Net 15 or Net 30 is standard)
- Payment method details

<Callout variant="info">
Keep records of all your UGC income. As a freelancer, you may need to report this on your taxes. Consider setting aside 20–30% of your earnings for tax purposes if you're in the US. Consult a tax professional for your specific situation.
</Callout>

## Red Flags in Brand Deals

Not every opportunity is a good one. Watch for these warning signs:

### 🚩 "We'll pay you in exposure"

Exposure doesn't pay rent. If a brand has budget for product development, marketing, and distribution, they have budget to pay creators. Politely decline.

### 🚩 Unreasonable deliverable requirements

A brand wants 10 videos, 20 photos, Stories coverage, and a blog post — for $100. The ask doesn't match the pay. Always calculate your effective hourly rate.

### 🚩 No contract or written agreement

Every deal should have something in writing — even if it's just a detailed email confirming deliverables, timeline, payment, and usage rights. If a brand refuses to put terms in writing, walk away.

### 🚩 "We'll pay after the content goes viral"

Your payment should not depend on performance (unless that's an *additional* bonus on top of a guaranteed base rate). You get paid for creating content, not for guaranteeing results.

### 🚩 Requesting full ownership with no extra compensation

If a brand wants to own your content outright (full buyout), that should cost significantly more than standard usage rights. Understand the difference:

- **Usage rights** = Brand can use the content for a specified period and purpose
- **Full buyout** = Brand owns the content permanently and can use it however they want

### 🚩 Extremely tight deadlines with no rush fee

"We need 5 videos by tomorrow" is a rush job and should be priced accordingly. Don't let urgency pressure you into accepting unfair terms.

## Negotiation Tips

Negotiation isn't confrontational — it's a conversation. Here's how to handle it confidently:

### Do your research

Before negotiating, know what similar creators charge. Check UGC rate databases, creator communities, and ask peers. Going into a negotiation informed is the #1 advantage.

### Lead with value

Instead of just stating your rate, explain what makes your content worth it:

> *"Based on my track record of creating high-engagement content in the [niche] space, and considering the deliverables and usage rights you're looking for, my rate would be $[X]."*

### The "package deal" play

If a brand pushes back on your per-video rate, offer a package:

> *"I understand the budget is tight. If we do a package of 4 videos, I can bring the per-video rate down to $[slightly lower] while giving you a consistent content pipeline."*

This wins because the brand gets a discount and you get more work guaranteed.

### Know your walk-away point

Before any negotiation, decide the lowest rate you'll accept. If the brand can't meet it, politely decline. There will always be more opportunities.

> *"I appreciate the offer, but that rate doesn't align with the quality and effort I put into my work. If the budget opens up in the future, I'd love to revisit this!"*

## When to Say No

Not every deal is worth taking. Say no when:

- The rate is below your minimum after negotiation
- The brand's values don't align with yours
- The deliverable requirements are unreasonable for the pay
- Something feels off — trust your instincts
- You're already overcommitted and quality would suffer
- The brand has a history of not paying creators (check online reviews)

<Callout variant="tip">
Saying no to bad deals creates space for good ones. Every hour you spend creating content for an underpaying brand is an hour you're not spending on building your portfolio, finding better clients, or creating content that grows your own audience. Your time is your most valuable asset — protect it.
</Callout>

## What's Next

You understand the money side. Now keep leveling up your content:

- **[Getting Started with UGC](/tutorials/getting-started)** — Revisit the fundamentals if you need a refresher
- **[Viral Video Formulas](/tutorials/viral-formulas)** — Better content = higher rates
- **Browse the [Jobs Board](/dashboard/jobs)** — Find real opportunities to put your skills to work

title: Content Creation Fundamentals
description: Equipment, lighting, filming techniques, and batch recording workflows — everything you need to create professional UGC with just your phone.
content:
You don't need a studio. You don't need expensive gear. You need your phone, decent lighting, and a system for creating content efficiently. This guide covers the fundamentals that separate amateur-looking content from professional UGC that brands want to pay for.

## Equipment: Start With What You Have

The best camera is the one in your pocket. Seriously — nearly all viral UGC is filmed on a smartphone. Brands actually *prefer* phone-shot content because it feels native to the platforms where it'll be posted.

### The essentials

**Your phone** — That's it. That's the most important piece of equipment. If it was made in the last 3–4 years, the camera is more than good enough.

**A clean lens** — This sounds obvious but it's the #1 reason videos look blurry or hazy. Wipe your camera lens with a soft cloth before every filming session. Your phone lives in your pocket, bag, and hands all day — the lens gets greasy.

<Callout variant="tip">
Before you film anything, wipe your lens. This single habit will instantly improve the quality of every video you make. Carry a small microfiber cloth or just use the corner of a clean t-shirt.
</Callout>

### Nice-to-have upgrades

Once you're consistently creating content and earning from it, consider these upgrades (in order of impact):

- **Ring light or desk lamp ($15–$30)** — Dramatically improves indoor video quality. Natural light is great but unpredictable. A simple ring light gives you consistent, flattering lighting any time of day.
- **Phone tripod ($10–$20)** — Stabilizes your shots and frees up your hands for demos. A basic one with a phone mount is all you need.
- **Wireless microphone ($25–$50)** — Important if you're doing voiceovers or talking directly to camera. Phone mics work but can pick up background noise.
- **Clip-on lens kit ($15–$25)** — Wide-angle lens is useful for showing products in context or filming in small spaces.

<Callout variant="warning">
Don't fall into the gear trap. New creators often use "I need better equipment" as an excuse not to start. You can create content that gets millions of views with a $200 phone and a window. Invest in gear only after you've proven you'll use it consistently.
</Callout>

## Lighting: The #1 Quality Factor

Lighting makes or breaks your video more than any other technical factor. Fortunately, great lighting is free.

### Natural light (free and best)

- **Face a window.** Position yourself so the window is in front of you (behind the camera). This gives you soft, even lighting on your face.
- **Avoid overhead light.** Ceiling lights create harsh shadows under your eyes and nose. Turn them off when you have good window light.
- **Shoot during "golden hours."** The best natural light is 1–2 hours after sunrise and 1–2 hours before sunset. But honestly, any daytime window light works great.
- **Overcast days are perfect.** Clouds act as a giant softbox, diffusing the light evenly.

### Indoor lighting tips

- **Two light sources > one.** If using artificial lights, place one in front of you and one slightly to the side. This eliminates harsh shadows.
- **Avoid mixed lighting.** Don't combine warm (yellowish) and cool (bluish) light sources — it makes your video look unnatural.
- **Ring lights are forgiving.** If you're unsure about lighting, a ring light placed directly behind your camera gives consistent, flattering results every time.

<Highlight emoji="💡" title="Quick lighting test">
Before filming, open your front-facing camera and check how you look. If one side of your face is noticeably darker than the other, adjust your position or add a light source. Your face should be evenly lit with no harsh shadows.
</Highlight>

## Filming Environment

Where you film matters. Your background tells a story — even if viewers don't consciously notice it.

### Indoor filming

- **Clean, uncluttered backgrounds.** A messy background is distracting. You don't need a fancy setup — just a tidy corner of your room.
- **Add visual interest.** A plant, a bookshelf, or even a simple colored wall is better than a blank white wall. Some texture and depth make your video more visually appealing.
- **Consistent "set."** Find one or two spots in your home that film well, and use them consistently. This saves setup time and creates a recognizable look for your content.

### Outdoor filming

- **Find shade.** Direct sunlight creates harsh shadows and makes you squint. Film under a tree, an awning, or on a porch.
- **Watch for wind.** Wind noise ruins audio. If it's windy, use a voiceover instead of live audio.
- **Be mindful of backgrounds.** No one wants to see a parking lot behind you (unless that's the vibe). Choose backgrounds that feel intentional.

## Batch Recording Workflow

This is the productivity hack that separates hobbyists from professionals. Instead of filming one video at a time, you batch record — filming multiple videos in a single session.

### Why batch recording works

- **Efficiency.** You only set up your filming environment once instead of every day.
- **Consistency.** Your lighting, outfit, and energy are consistent across videos.
- **Less decision fatigue.** Plan everything in advance, then just execute.
- **Buffer content.** Having 5–10 videos in drafts means you can post daily without filming daily.

### The batch recording process

<Step number={1} title="Plan your content (15 min)">
Decide what videos you're filming. Write out your hooks, key points, and CTAs for each video. Aim for 5–10 videos per batch session.
</Step>

<Step number={2} title="Set up your environment (10 min)">
Clean your background, set up lighting, clean your lens, charge your phone. Put it on Do Not Disturb mode.
</Step>

<Step number={3} title="Film everything (30–60 min)">
Run through your video list. Film each one 2–3 times so you have options in editing. Don't worry about perfection — you'll pick the best take later.
</Step>

<Step number={4} title="Save as drafts">
Upload each video to TikTok (or your primary platform) as a draft. Add captions, hashtags, and sounds later. Now you have a bank of content ready to post throughout the week.
</Step>

<Callout variant="tip">
Batch record in the same outfit? Film in a few different outfits during one session. Change your top between batches of 2–3 videos so it doesn't look like you filmed everything at once. A quick wardrobe swap takes 30 seconds.
</Callout>

## Posting Cadence

How often you post matters — not just for audience growth, but for how the algorithm treats your account.

### Recommended schedule

- **Minimum:** 1 video per day
- **Sweet spot:** 2–3 videos per day
- **Spacing:** Wait at least 2 hours between posts

<Callout variant="warning">
Posting multiple videos within an hour can trigger platform penalties. TikTok's algorithm may suppress your reach if it thinks you're spamming. Space your posts at least 2 hours apart — set reminders if you need to.
</Callout>

### When to post

The "best time to post" depends on your audience, but here are general guidelines:

- **Morning:** 7–9 AM (people checking phones before work/school)
- **Lunch:** 11 AM – 1 PM (break time scrolling)
- **Evening:** 7–10 PM (prime time — most engagement happens here)

Start with these windows and adjust based on your analytics after 2–3 weeks.

## Audio Strategy

Sound is half the experience on short-form platforms. Your audio choice directly impacts your reach.

### Trending sounds

- **Use trending sounds when possible.** The algorithm boosts content that uses popular audio.
- **How to find them:** Browse your For You Page and notice which sounds keep appearing. Use TikTok's "trending" filter in the sound library.
- **Match the vibe.** A trending sound only helps if it fits your content. Don't force a comedic sound on a serious product demo.

### Original audio

- **Use for voiceovers and tutorials.** When you're explaining something, original audio is often more effective than trending sounds.
- **Speak clearly and at a good pace.** Not too fast, not too slow. Practice your voiceover before recording.
- **Keep background noise minimal.** Film in a quiet space. Close windows, turn off fans, and put your phone on silent.

## Video Quality Checklist

Before you post *any* video, run through this checklist:

<Checklist>
  <ChecklistItem>Lens is clean — no smudges or haze</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Lighting is even — no harsh shadows on your face</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Background is tidy and intentional</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Audio is clear — no background noise, wind, or echo</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Video is in focus — especially the product or main subject</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Text on screen is readable and stays up long enough</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Hook grabs attention in the first 2–3 seconds</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Video is the right aspect ratio (9:16 vertical for all short-form platforms)</ChecklistItem>
</Checklist>

## Weekly Content Calendar

Here's a simple template for planning your week:

| Day | Content Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Product demo / review | Lead with your strongest content |
| Tuesday | Tutorial / how-to | Educational content builds trust |
| Wednesday | Trending format adaptation | Ride a current trend with your niche twist |
| Thursday | Before/after or transformation | High visual impact |
| Friday | Personal story / opinion | Build audience connection |
| Saturday | Batch film next week's content | Preparation day |
| Sunday | Engage + respond to comments | Community building |

<Callout variant="info">
This is a starting framework, not a rigid rule. Adapt it based on what performs well for your audience. After 2–3 weeks of posting, your analytics will tell you which content types get the most engagement.
</Callout>

## What's Next

You've got the fundamentals down. Time to learn the formulas that make content go viral:

- **[Viral Video Formulas](/tutorials/viral-formulas)** — The Hook → Demo → CTA framework and more
- **[Hook Library](/tutorials/hook-library)** — 30+ plug-and-play hooks for any niche
- **[Discoverability](/tutorials/discoverability)** — Hashtags, captions, and getting found

title: Discoverability: Hashtags, Captions & SEO
description: How to get your content found — hashtag strategy, keyword-rich captions, trending audio, and cross-platform tactics.
content:
Creating great content is step one. Getting it *found* is step two. Discoverability is the art and science of making sure the right people see your videos — not just your followers, but the millions of potential viewers who are searching, scrolling, and discovering new creators every day.

This guide covers hashtags, captions, trending audio, TikTok SEO, and cross-platform strategies.

## Hashtag Strategy

Hashtags are still one of the primary ways platforms categorize and distribute your content. But there's a big difference between throwing random hashtags on a post and having a real strategy.

### How hashtags actually work

When you add a hashtag, you're essentially telling the platform: *"Put my video in this category."* The algorithm then shows your video to people who have engaged with content in that category.

The right hashtags = showing your video to people who are *already interested* in your topic.
The wrong hashtags = showing your video to people who will scroll right past it.

### The tiered hashtag approach

Use a mix of hashtag sizes to maximize reach:

| Tier | Size | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Big | 1M+ posts | Broad reach, high competition | #skincare, #fitness, #cooking |
| Medium | 100K–1M posts | Targeted reach, moderate competition | #skincareforbeginners, #homeworkout |
| Small/Niche | 10K–100K posts | Highly targeted, lower competition | #drugstoreskincare, #5minutemeals |
| Micro | Under 10K posts | Very specific, almost guaranteed visibility | #morningskincareroutine2026 |

### The formula

For each post, use **5–7 hashtags** with this mix:

- 1–2 big hashtags (reach)
- 2–3 medium hashtags (targeting)
- 2 small/niche hashtags (precision)

<Callout variant="tip">
More isn't better. Using 20+ hashtags looks spammy and can actually reduce your reach. Stick to 5–7 highly relevant tags. Quality over quantity, always.
</Callout>

### How to research hashtags

<Step number={1} title="Start with your niche keyword">
Type your main keyword into TikTok/Instagram search. Look at the suggested hashtags that appear — these are what people are actively searching for.
</Step>

<Step number={2} title="Check competitor content">
Look at the top-performing videos in your niche. What hashtags are they using? These are proven to work in your space.
</Step>

<Step number={3} title="Build a hashtag bank">
Create a note on your phone with 20–30 relevant hashtags organized by tier. For each post, you'll pick 5–7 from this bank instead of brainstorming from scratch.
</Step>

### Hashtags to avoid

- **Banned or flagged hashtags** — Some hashtags are shadowbanned. If you notice a sudden drop in reach, try removing a hashtag and reposting.
- **Completely unrelated hashtags** — Using #viral or #foryou doesn't help if your content has nothing to do with those broad categories. (That said, on TikTok, #fyp is still commonly used as a discovery tag.)
- **Brand-specific hashtags you're not affiliated with** — Don't tag a brand in your post unless you're actually working with them or reviewing their product.

## Caption Strategy

Captions aren't just descriptions — they're a discoverability tool. Platforms use the text in your captions to understand what your content is about and who to show it to.

### Keyword-rich captions

Write captions that naturally include terms people search for:

> ❌ *"Try this!! 😍"*

> ✅ *"My morning skincare routine using only drugstore products — SPF included ☀️"*

The second caption tells the algorithm exactly what the video is about. Anyone searching for "morning skincare routine" or "drugstore skincare" might discover your content.

### Caption formulas

**The Keyword-Loaded:**
> *"[Primary keyword] that [benefit] — perfect for [target audience]"*
> Example: "Quick meal prep ideas that actually taste good — perfect for busy weekdays"

**The Story Tease:**
> *"I've been using [product/method] for [time period] and [result]... [call to action]"*
> Example: "I've been using this planner for 3 months and my productivity doubled... watch till the end to see my setup"

**The Question:**
> *"Has anyone else tried [product/method]? Here's what happened when I did 👇"*
> Example: "Has anyone else tried ice rolling? Here's what happened when I did 👇"

### The brand name trick

<Callout variant="tip">
When creating UGC for a brand, **don't mention the brand name in your caption.** Instead, put it in the comments. This creates a natural engagement loop — people see your content, get curious, and either ask "What is that?" or find the answer in the comments. This approach makes the content feel more organic and less like an ad, which helps it perform better algorithmically.
</Callout>

## Trending Audio Strategy

Audio is a major factor in how platforms distribute your content. Using the right audio at the right time can significantly boost your reach.

### How to find trending sounds

- **Browse your FYP.** When you notice the same sound appearing in multiple videos, it's trending.
- **Check the sounds library.** TikTok's sound library has a "trending" section that shows what's popular right now.
- **Follow trend-tracking accounts.** Several creators specialize in posting trending sounds before they peak.
- **Look at the arrow icon.** On TikTok, trending sounds show a small arrow icon next to the sound name.

### When to use trending audio

**Use trending audio when:**
- The sound matches your content's mood or message
- You're creating a trend-based video (POV, transition, etc.)
- You want maximum algorithmic boost
- The sound is on the way up (early adoption gets the most benefit)

**Use original audio when:**
- You're doing a voiceover or tutorial
- The content relies on what you're saying
- There's no trending sound that fits naturally
- You're creating a product demo where the viewer needs to hear you speak

### Matching audio to content type

| Content Type | Best Audio |
|---|---|
| Product demo with explanation | Original voiceover |
| Before/after transformation | Trending audio (dramatic/upbeat) |
| POV / relatable content | Trending audio (relevant to the vibe) |
| Tutorial / how-to | Original voiceover or calm background music |
| Unboxing / first impressions | Original audio (genuine reactions) |
| Aesthetic / lifestyle | Trending audio (chill/moody) |

## TikTok SEO Basics

TikTok is increasingly becoming a *search engine*, especially for younger users. Optimizing your content for search (SEO) means your videos can be discovered through TikTok's search bar — not just the FYP.

### How TikTok SEO works

TikTok analyzes several signals to determine what your video is about:

- **On-screen text** — The words that appear in your video
- **Voiceover/speech** — What you say (TikTok transcribes audio)
- **Caption text** — Your written caption
- **Hashtags** — Topic categorization
- **Sounds** — What audio is associated with your content

### SEO optimization checklist

<Checklist>
  <ChecklistItem>Include your main keyword in the on-screen text</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Say the keyword out loud if doing a voiceover</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Use the keyword naturally in your caption</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Add 2–3 relevant hashtags that include the keyword or variations</ChecklistItem>
  <ChecklistItem>Use a descriptive title/first line that matches what people would search</ChecklistItem>
</Checklist>

### Example: SEO-optimized video

**Niche:** Skincare
**Target keyword:** "morning skincare routine"

- **On-screen text:** "My 5-minute morning skincare routine"
- **Voiceover:** "Here's my morning skincare routine that takes less than 5 minutes..."
- **Caption:** "The morning skincare routine that cleared my skin — all drugstore products ☀️"
- **Hashtags:** #morningskincare #skincareroutine #drugstoreskincare #skincaretips #spf

<Highlight emoji="🔍" title="Think like a searcher">
Before creating content, ask yourself: "What would someone type into the TikTok search bar to find this?" That phrase is your target keyword. Use it in your text, voiceover, and caption.
</Highlight>

## Cross-Platform Strategy

Creating content for multiple platforms doesn't mean starting from scratch each time. It means being smart about how you repurpose and distribute.

### The repurposing workflow

<Step number={1} title="Create for TikTok first">
TikTok is the most native format for short-form UGC. Create your video here first with no platform-specific watermarks.
</Step>

<Step number={2} title="Save the clean version">
Before posting, save the video to your camera roll *without* the TikTok watermark. You can also use your original recording before adding TikTok-specific effects.
</Step>

<Step number={3} title="Adapt captions and hashtags for each platform">
TikTok and Instagram have different hashtag cultures. Don't just copy-paste — adjust your caption and hashtags for each platform's norms.
</Step>

<Step number={4} title="Stagger your posts">
Don't post to all three platforms at the same time. Post to TikTok first, then Instagram Reels 4–6 hours later, then YouTube Shorts the next day.
</Step>

### Platform-specific adjustments

**TikTok → Instagram Reels:**
- Remove any TikTok watermark
- Slightly more polished caption
- Fewer hashtags (Instagram tends to use 5–10 vs TikTok's broader approach)
- Add to relevant Stories for extra reach

**TikTok → YouTube Shorts:**
- Remove TikTok watermark
- Write a clear, search-optimized title (YouTube is search-first)
- Add a description with keywords
- YouTube doesn't use hashtags the same way — focus on title and description

<Callout variant="warning">
All three platforms actively penalize content with competitor watermarks. A TikTok video with a visible TikTok watermark will get suppressed on Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts. Always save and repost the clean version.
</Callout>

## What's Next

You're discoverable. Now make sure you're compensated fairly:

- **[Compensation Guide](/tutorials/compensation-guide)** — Understand rates, negotiate deals, and know your worth
- **[Community Management](/tutorials/community-management)** — Turn new viewers into loyal followers
- **[Viral Video Formulas](/tutorials/viral-formulas)** — Create content that earns the reach you're optimizing for

title: Where to find paid UGC jobs and compare opportunities
description: Find UGC creator jobs through public boards, brand briefs, and direct outreach. Use a practical checklist to compare pay, deliverables, and application routes.
content:
## Where can you find paid UGC jobs?

You can find paid UGC jobs on public creator job boards, brand career pages, agency casting calls, and through direct outreach. Start with a written brief that states compensation, deliverables, eligibility, and an application destination. A request for content is not automatically a paid opportunity: affiliate commissions, performance bonuses, and free products have different payment terms.

[ugc.community](/jobs) is a public UGC job board that brings reviewed external opportunities and directly submitted brand briefs into one searchable feed. Creators can browse without an account or a subscription. Use the [guaranteed cash filter](/jobs?pay=cash) to look for listings categorized as cash compensation, then read the full terms before applying. Available roles change; a search may have no current matches.

## Which discovery channel fits your search?

| Channel | Useful when | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public UGC job board | You want to compare several briefs in one place | Source, closing date, compensation category, and original application link |
| Brand career or creator page | You already know which brand you want to work with | Whether the role involves creating assets, posting to your audience, or both |
| Agency casting call | You want a specific campaign or production role | The hiring agency, client, location, schedule, and payment responsibility |
| Direct outreach | Your samples match a brand but no suitable brief is public | Whether the brand is accepting pitches and who manages creator work |

These are complementary routes. A job board helps with discovery; the hiring party still decides whom to hire and on what terms. This guide is published by ugc.community and describes its own board alongside other ways to find work.

## How do you search ugc.community?

1. Open the [public jobs feed](/jobs). Try a product category such as skincare, food, or fitness using the keyword search.
2. Compare guaranteed cash listings with [base plus variable pay](/jobs?pay=mixed) if both fit your goals. Keep the fixed amount separate from possible bonuses.
3. Read deliverables, eligibility, usage rights, and closing dates. Treat any missing field as a question for the hiring party.
4. Follow the listing's application route. Some jobs accept email applications through the site; others send you to the original destination.

A creator account lets you save a [reusable application profile](/apply-profile) with work links and use it for jobs that accept email applications. Browsing does not require signing in.

## What should you compare before applying?

Record the same fields for every opportunity:

- **Guaranteed payment:** the fixed amount, currency, payment trigger, and expected payment date.
- **Deliverables:** video count, duration, aspect ratio, raw footage, hooks, and revision rounds.
- **Eligibility:** country, language, age requirements, shipping availability, and filming location.
- **Usage:** where the brand wants to publish the work, whether it includes ads, and the requested duration.
- **Application:** the destination, requested samples, deadline, and hiring contact.

A larger headline payment may cover more work or broader usage. Compare the scope before deciding which brief fits. Use the [compensation comparison guide](/tutorials/compare-ugc-compensation) for an example that separates fixed pay from variable earnings.

## How are listings reviewed and kept current?

ugc.community reviews listings before publication. External opportunities identify their source and link to the original destination. Missing terms are marked as not stated. Listings honor their closing dates; external opportunities also expire seven days after their last manual freshness review unless reviewed again.
